function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repo.  
It contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node 18 image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment (2 replicas) |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | ClusterIP service exposing the app |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main` |

> **NOTE** – The repo is a Node.js project, so the Docker base image is `node:18‑alpine`.  
> If you prefer a different Node version, just change the `FROM` line.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Use the official lightweight Node 18 image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` keeps the image small.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the default port used by most Node apps.

---

## 2. Kubernetes manifests

Create a folder called `k8s` (or any name you prefer) and add the two files below.

### 2.1 `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

### 2.2 `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Two replicas give you basic high‑availability.  
> * The service maps port 80 (inside the cluster) to the app’s port 3000.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add `ci.yml`.

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        docker tag zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Push Docker image
      run: |
        docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

### Secrets you’ll need

| Secret | What to put |
|--------|-------------|
| `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` | Your Docker Hub username |
| `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` | A Docker Hub *access token* (not your password) |

> **Tip** – In the repo settings → Secrets → Actions, add those two secrets.

---

## 4. Add, commit, push

```bash
# From the repo root
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it!  
Once pushed, the workflow will run automatically, build the image, and push it to Docker Hub.  
You can then deploy to any Kubernetes cluster with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image tags, or service type as your environment requires. Happy coding!
